title: The bow and the grey iron: 'a contest and the beginning of death'
greek: ἀέθλια καὶ φόνου ἀρχήν (aethlia kai phonou archēn); πολιὸς σίδηρος (polios sidēros)
short: The book's first lines announce that Penelope's archery contest will also be the start of the slaughter, so the audience watches every suitor's attempt knowing the outcome.
body: Athena puts the idea into Penelope's mind, but the plan was Penelope's own: she proposed the contest to the disguised Odysseus at 19.570-81. The 'grey iron' (polios sidēros) is the set of twelve iron axe-heads through which the arrow must pass. Monro explains aethlia here as 'the material of a contest', the objects that make it up, not the prize. The phrase phonou archē, 'beginning of slaughter', is a narrator's forecast of the kind Homer uses at turning points, and the whole line returns, in the mouth of the dead suitor Amphimedon, at 24.168-9, where he adds that the plan was Odysseus' own. The repetition frames Books XXI to XXIV: the contest set up here is the event the dead are still explaining in Hades.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 21.3

title: The bent bronze key and the store-room door
greek: κληῒς εὐκαμπής (klēis eukampēs); ὀχεύς (ocheus, bolt); ἱμάς (himas, thong)
short: A curved bronze key with an ivory handle, pushed through a slot to knock back the inside bolt: Homer's most precise description of a lock.
body: Monro reconstructs the mechanism. The bolt (ocheus) was on the inside of the door and could be drawn from outside by a leather thong passed through a slit; when the door was shut, the thong was tied to a hook or handle (korōnē) outside. To open it, Penelope first unties the thong, then pushes the curved key through the opening and 'aims' it (antha tituskomenē, Murray's 'with sure aim') so that it knocks the bolts back. The verb of aiming is the same one used of shooting an arrow (21.421), and it may be no accident that the scene of the bow begins with a woman taking aim. The store-room is 'far remote' (eschatos) and rarely opened, which is why the doors groan like a bull (21.48-50). Compare the shorter description of Eurycleia locking a door at 1.441-2.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 21.46-48

title: Back-bent bow (toxon palintonon)
greek: τόξον παλίντονον (toxon palintonon)
short: Palintonos, 'stretched back', may simply describe any bow that springs back when drawn, or a particular recurved type; ancient and modern scholars disagree.
body: Murray's 'back-bent' renders palintonos, literally 'back-stretched'. Monro sets out the two possibilities. It may be a general epithet for the way a bow springs back when released, or it may name a specific design, as when Herodotus (7.69) uses it of Arabian bows: a recurved bow whose limbs curve away from the archer when it is unstrung, so that stringing it takes great force and skill. That would suit the story, in which young men fail even to bend it. The bow of Odysseus is also a horn bow (21.395), like Pandarus' bow made from the horns of a wild goat (Il. 4.105-11), which supports the composite, recurved reading. The word reappears in one ancient quotation of the philosopher Heraclitus, who speaks of a 'back-stretched harmony, as of the bow and the lyre' (fr. B51 Diels-Kranz), a pairing this book itself makes when Odysseus strings the bow like a singer stringing a lyre (21.406-9).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 21.11

title: Arrows 'fraught with groanings' (stonoentes oistoi)
greek: στονόεντες ὀϊστοί (stonoentes oistoi)
short: The arrows are called 'groaning' because of the groans they will cause; the epithet hangs over the contest from its first lines.
body: Stonoeis means 'full of groans, causing groans'. Monro remarks that 'the groans which the arrow may cause are regarded as something that is inherent in it': the quality of the outcome is transferred to the weapon. The formula is repeated when Penelope carries the quiver into the hall (21.60) and again by the dead Amphimedon describing the massacre (24.180), so it acts as a small refrain across the end of the poem. The same habit of thought appears in Eurymachus' phrase 'the arrows that bring swift death' (ōkumoroi, 22.75), on which Monro makes the same point. For a reader of the Iliad the word recalls the stonoenta belea, 'groaning missiles', of battle scenes (e.g. Il. 8.159).

title: Iphitus son of Eurytus, giver of the bow
greek: Ἴφιτος Εὐρυτίδης (Iphitos Eurytidēs)
short: The bow came to Odysseus as a guest-gift from Iphitus, whose father Eurytus was a great archer, and whose own story ends in the betrayal of hospitality.
body: The narrator pauses to give the bow a pedigree, as the Iliad does for Agamemnon's sceptre (Il. 2.101-8). It belonged to Eurytus of Oechalia, an archer so proud that he challenged Apollo and was killed for it (Od. 8.223-8); his son Iphitus gave it to the young Odysseus when they met in Messene, receiving a sword and spear in return. Iphitus was searching for twelve stolen mares, and found his death at the house of Heracles, who killed him although he was his guest and kept the horses. Later mythographers tell the story more fully: Apollodorus (2.6.1-2) and Sophocles (Trachiniae 269-73) say Heracles threw him from the walls of Tiryns. The digression thus attaches to the weapon of vengeance a story about the gravest crime against a guest, the very crime of which the suitors are guilty in Odysseus' house.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 21.26

title: Heracles the guest-killer: 'the table which he had set before him'
greek: οὐδὲ θεῶν ὄπιν ᾐδέσατ' οὐδὲ τράπεζαν (oude theōn opin aidesat' oude trapezan)
short: Heracles killed Iphitus after sharing his table with him, ignoring both the gods' watchful anger and the sacred bond created by a shared meal.
body: In Homeric guest-friendship (xenia) to eat at a man's table creates a bond protected by Zeus Xenios; to kill a guest is a crime against the gods (opis, 'the regard' or watchful vengeance of the gods). Murray's 'had regard neither for the wrath of the gods nor for the table' renders aideomai, the verb of respect and shame (aidōs). Heracles is called here 'well versed in great deeds' (megalōn epiistora ergōn), a phrase Monro finds hard to pin down: epiistōr seems related to histōr, 'one who judges', and he refuses to make megala erga simply mean 'deeds of violence'. The story is sharply relevant. Odysseus and Iphitus 'never knew one another at the table' (21.35-6), because death intervened; the suitors, who eat daily at Odysseus' table while abusing his house, are about to discover what follows from despising it.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 21.26

title: Messene and the young Odysseus' embassy
greek: Μεσσήνη (Messēnē); ἐξεσίη (exesiē, embassy); χρεῖος (chreios, debt)
short: Messene in the south-western Peloponnese, where the young Odysseus went on a public mission to recover 300 sheep and their shepherds stolen by Messenian raiders.
body: Monro notes that the passage treats Messenia as part of Lacedaemon: the meeting is said to happen 'in Lacedaemon' (21.13) and 'in Messene', at the house of Ortilochus, who lived at Pherae (3.488-9). The episode gives a rare glimpse of Odysseus before Troy. Cattle- and sheep-raiding by sea was a normal, honourable activity between communities, and recovering stolen stock was a duty owed to the whole people: the debt was owed 'by the whole people' (pas dēmos), and Laertes and the elders sent the youth out on an embassy (exesiē). Nestor's long story of a cattle raid on Elis to recover a debt (Il. 11.670-761) is the closest parallel. The detail anticipates Odysseus' own plan to restock his farms by raiding (23.357-8).

title: The bow as a keepsake of a guest-friend
greek: μνῆμα ξείνοιο φίλοιο (mnēma xeinoio philoio)
short: Odysseus never took this bow to Troy but kept it at home as a memorial of his guest-friend, so it belongs to Ithaca and its master.
body: Gifts exchanged between guest-friends were tangible records of the relationship, and were kept and named. Menelaus offers Telemachus a cup so that he will 'remember me all his days' (4.591-2), and Helen gives a robe as 'a memorial of Helen's hands' (mnēm' Helenēs cheirōn, 15.125-7); in the Iliad Glaucus and Diomedes refuse to fight once they discover their grandfathers' guest-friendship, and exchange armour (Il. 6.215-36). The bow is thus a mnēma, a 'reminder', of a friendship cut short by Heracles' crime. Its staying at home matters for the plot: it could not have been lost with his ships, and only the true master of the house can use it. Odysseus 'carried it in his own land', so stringing it is a claim to that land.

title: Simile: the doors bellow like a bull
greek: ἀνέβραχεν ἠΰτε ταῦρος βοσκόμενος λειμῶνι (anebrachen ēute tauros boskomenos leimōni)
short: The long-unopened store-room doors roar as the key strikes the bolt, compared with a bull bellowing in a meadow.
body: One of the briefest similes in the poem, it turns a domestic sound into something loud and animal. Monro observes that the creaking of the lock 'reminds us that it has not been opened for a long time', since Odysseus left: the bow has been shut away for twenty years. The verb bracheīn is used in the Iliad of the clash of armour and the roar of a wounded Ares (Il. 5.859, 863), so the noise of the door has a martial ring as the weapon of revenge is brought out. The sound effect prepares a series of significant noises in this book: Penelope's weeping over the bow (21.55-7), the bowstring that 'sings' like a swallow (21.411), and Zeus' thunder (21.413).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 21.48

title: The twelve axes: what was the shot?
greek: πελέκεων δυοκαίδεκα (pelekeōn duokaideka); διοϊστεύειν σιδήρου (dioisteuein sidērou)
short: The winner must string the bow and shoot through a row of twelve axes; exactly how the arrow passed 'through the iron' has been debated since antiquity.
body: Penelope describes the feat at 19.572-81: Odysseus used to set the axes in a row 'like the props (drūochoi) of a ship' and shoot through them from far off. Since the arrow 'did not miss the end of the handle' of any (21.421-2), Monro concludes that each axe-head must have had a hole or opening and that the twelve openings were set in line to form a kind of tube. He reports Helbig's two candidate shapes (a double axe with round holes between the blades, and a perforated crescent-shaped axe) and favours a third, the Mycenaean axe from Vaphio with two large holes, as actual evidence from the Homeric world. Others have imagined holes for the haft or rings at the end of the handles; no solution commands agreement. Telemachus plants the axes in a trench in the earthen floor of the hall (21.120-3), which Monro takes as proof that the contest happened indoors.

title: Telemachus almost strings the bow
greek: τρὶς μέν μιν πελέμιξεν (tris men min pelemixen)
short: Telemachus tries three times and would have succeeded on the fourth, but a nod from Odysseus stops him; the scene shows he has grown into his father's strength.
body: The pattern 'three times... and the fourth time' is a standard Homeric way of marking a climax that is then checked (compare Patroclus at the wall of Troy, Il. 16.702-6). Monro notes that line 125 is borrowed from Il. 21.176, where it describes the effort of pulling a spear from the ground. Telemachus' success would have spoiled the plan, and might have made the contest, by Penelope's terms, end with no claim on her. His earlier words are full of irony: if he wins, he says, he will not mind his mother leaving, since he will be able to wield his father's battle-gear (21.113-17). Monro, in his additional notes, reads this as reassurance to the suitors that his success would not affect them. The quiet nod of refusal (ananeue) is the first sign in the hall of the silent understanding between father and son.

title: Leiodes the suitors' soothsayer
greek: Λειώδης Οἴνοπος υἱός, θυοσκόος (Leiōdēs Oinopos huios, thuoskoos)
short: The first suitor to try the bow is their seer, who disliked their outrages; his prediction that the bow will kill many princes comes true unintentionally.
body: A thuoskoos was a seer who read the signs of burnt sacrifice; Leiodes sits by the mixing-bowl in the inner part of the hall, perhaps because he poured the libations. His soft 'unworn' hands fail at once. In despair he says the bow will rob many princes 'of spirit and of life' (21.153-4); Monro notes how fitting it is that this unconscious prophecy comes from a professional prophet. Monro also cites a later parallel from Pausanias (6.8.4): the retired athlete Timanthes tested his strength daily with a great bow, and when he found he could no longer draw it, burned himself on a pyre. Monro explains the name as an Ionic form related to lēos, 'people'. Leiodes' fate is told at 22.310-29, where his claim to innocence does not save him.

title: Odysseus reveals himself to Eumaeus and Philoetius
greek: οὐλή (oulē, scar); σῆμα ἀριφραδές (sēma ariphrades, manifest sign)
short: While the suitors struggle with the bow, Odysseus slips outside, tests the loyalty of the two herdsmen, and proves his identity by the boar's scar.
body: This is one of a chain of recognitions that structures the second half of the poem: Telemachus (16), the dog Argus (17), Eurycleia by the scar (19), the herdsmen here, Penelope by the bed (23) and Laertes by the scar and the orchard (24). Each uses a different sign (sēma), and Odysseus always tests before he reveals. Monro points out that the scene happens while Antinous and Eurymachus are 'still busy with the bow' (so he would start the paragraph at 21.186), which keeps the hall's attention elsewhere. The promise of wives, property and a house next to his own, so that the two slaves will be 'comrades and brothers of Telemachus' (21.214-16), is an extraordinary offer of near-kinship to loyal slaves. The scar story itself was told at 19.392-466.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 21.186

title: The festival of Apollo the archer
greek: ἑορτὴ τοῖο θεοῖο ἁγνή (heortē toio theoio hagnē); Ἀπόλλων κλυτότοξος (Apollōn klytotoxos)
short: The slaughter takes place on a holy feast-day of Apollo, god of archery, which Antinous uses as an excuse to postpone the contest.
body: Antinous claims that on such a holy day no one should bend a bow, and proposes sacrificing goats to 'Apollo of the famous bow' next morning before trying again. Monro identifies the feast as that of the new moon, sacred to Apollo, prepared for earlier in the book's prelude (20.156, 20.276-8; cf. Odysseus' oath that he will return 'as this moon wanes and the next begins', 14.162 and 19.307). He notes that the epithet klytotoxos is 'used here with meaning': a contest of the bow should be preceded by honours to the bow-god. The irony is heavy. The festival of the archer god is the day on which the archer returns; Odysseus calls his first killing shot a target 'if Apollo grant me glory' (22.7), and the suitors had prayed to Apollo against Eumaeus (21.364-5).

title: The Centaur Eurytion at the wedding of Peirithous
greek: Κένταυρος ἀγακλυτὸς Εὐρυτίων (Kentauros agaklytos Eurytiōn); Λαπίθαι (Lapithai)
short: Antinous warns the beggar with the tale of a drunken Centaur mutilated for outrage in his host's house: a myth that fits the suitors better than Odysseus.
body: Eurytion came to the Lapiths as a guest of their king Peirithous, was 'blinded' (aase) by wine and did violence in his host's house; the heroes dragged him out and cut off his ears and nose, and from this came the feud between Centaurs and men. Later tradition placed the episode at Peirithous' wedding, where the Centaur seized the bride: Pausanias (5.10.8) describes it on the west pediment of the temple of Zeus at Olympia, and Ovid tells the battle at length (Metamorphoses 12.210-535). In the Iliad Nestor remembers fighting alongside Peirithous against the 'mountain beasts' (Il. 1.262-8; cf. 2.742-4). The exemplum backfires: it is the suitors who are the drunken, violent guests, and the punishment of ears and nostrils cut off with the pitiless bronze will be inflicted, in the same words, on Melanthius (22.475-6). Monro notes that aaō is used especially of mental damage.

title: 'The bow shall be for men': Telemachus echoes Hector
greek: ἱστόν τ' ἠλακάτην τε... τόξον δ' ἄνδρεσσι μελήσει (histon t' ēlakatēn te... toxon d' andressi melēsei)
short: Telemachus sends Penelope back to her weaving with words adapted from Hector's farewell to Andromache, replacing 'war' with 'the bow'.
body: Hector tells Andromache to go home to 'the loom and the distaff', for 'war shall be the concern of men' (Il. 6.490-3). Telemachus has already used the formula once, about 'speech' (muthos) at 1.356-9; here he substitutes 'the bow'. Monro argues that both Odyssean versions adapt the Iliad, and that here the words are 'distinctly inappropriate', since the bow was in Penelope's keeping and the contest was her idea. He suggests the poet intended an ironic double meaning: the bow will indeed be 'the concern of the men, all of them', in a way the suitors do not foresee. The dismissal also has a practical function, as Monro notes: it removes Penelope from the hall before the killing, so that she sleeps through it (21.356-8) and the recognition scene of Book XXIII can follow.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 21.350-358

title: A ship's cable of papyrus
greek: ὅπλον νεὸς βύβλινον (hoplon neos byblinon)
short: Philoetius ties the courtyard gate shut with a ship's rope made of papyrus fibre, sealing the suitors in.
body: Bublinos means 'made of bublos', the Egyptian papyrus plant, whose fibre was used for rope, sails and caulking (Herodotus 2.92, 2.96). Herodotus also records that when Xerxes bridged the Hellespont, the Phoenicians supplied cables of flax and the Egyptians cables of papyrus (7.34). That such a cable lies in the portico of an Ithacan house is a small sign of long-distance trade in the world of the poem. The rope has a grim double in the next book: the cable of a dark-prowed ship is used to hang the disloyal maids (22.465-7). Monro explains the verb epedēse as 'made fast', the prefix epi- being used of shutting, and places the portico (aithousa) over the gateway of the court.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 21.390-391

anchor: worms might have eaten the horns
title: A horn bow: 'lest worms had eaten the horns'
greek: μὴ κέρα ἶπες ἔδοιεν (mē kera ipes edoien)
short: Odysseus turns the bow this way and that to check whether woodworm has damaged its horn parts during twenty years of disuse.
body: The detail shows that the bow is a composite weapon with horn in its construction, like Pandarus' bow, made from the horns of a wild goat joined by a craftsman (Il. 4.105-11). Such bows needed care, which also explains the suitors' warming and greasing of it before their attempts (21.176-80). Ipes (singular ips) are wood- or horn-boring grubs. The careful inspection is the action of an expert, and the suitors read it correctly while drawing the wrong conclusion: one calls him 'a connoisseur and a sly one with bows' (thēētēr kai epiklopos), which Monro glosses as 'a sort of fancier and connoisseur', a word used 'in a good or at least an indulgent sense'. Another wishes he may get as much profit as he will be able to string the bow, a wish fulfilled in the opposite sense (Monro on 402-3).

title: Simile: the archer as singer stringing a lyre
greek: ὡς ὅτ' ἀνὴρ φόρμιγγος ἐπιστάμενος καὶ ἀοιδῆς (hōs hot' anēr phorminx epistamenos kai aoidēs)
short: Odysseus strings the great bow as effortlessly as a bard fits a new string to his lyre: the climax of the contest is compared to an act of song.
body: The phorminx was the bard's lyre, and the simile joins the poem's two great arts, fighting and singing. Odysseus has already been praised for telling his story 'like a singer' (11.368), and throughout the poem he narrates, invents and performs; now his decisive deed is likened to the tuning of an instrument. The sheep-gut string (enteron oios) twisted on a peg (kollops) gives a precise technical picture. Monro records Tyrrell's conjecture heōi ('his own') for neōi ('new') peg. The pairing of bow and lyre, both stringed and both under Apollo's patronage, was later made famous by Heraclitus' image of a harmony 'of the bow and the lyre' (fr. B51). The bard Phemius, who sings among the suitors, is about to plead with the archer for his life (22.330-53).

anchor: like to a swallow in tone
title: The bowstring sings like a swallow
greek: ἡ δ' ὑπὸ καλὸν ἄεισε, χελιδόνι εἰκέλη αὐδήν (hē d' hupo kalon aeise, chelidoni eikelē audēn)
short: Testing the string, Odysseus makes it 'sing' with a sound like a swallow's voice: a musical note that continues the lyre simile.
body: The verb aeidō, 'sing', is the word for a bard's song, so the bowstring becomes a singer in its turn. Monro takes hupo as 'in answer to his touch'. The swallow returns in the next book, when Athena flies up to the roof-beam of the hall and sits there 'like a swallow' to watch the battle (22.239-40); readers have connected the two passages, so that the sound of the string and the presence of the goddess are linked. The swallow is also the bird that marks the coming of spring (Hesiod, Works and Days 568-9), and the action takes place at a festival of the new moon. The note of the string, the suitors' change of colour and Zeus' thunder follow in quick succession, a sequence of signs that the tide has turned.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 21.411

title: Zeus' thunder and 'crooked-counselling' Cronos
greek: Ζεὺς δὲ μεγάλ' ἔκτυπε σήματα φαίνων (Zeus de megal' ektupe sēmata phainōn); Κρόνου πάϊς ἀγκυλομήτεω (Kronou pais ankylomēteō)
short: As the bow is strung, Zeus thunders as a sign of favour; Odysseus rejoices that 'the son of crooked-counselling Cronos' has sent him an omen.
body: Thunder from Zeus is a recognised sign (sēma, teras). On the morning of this day Odysseus had prayed for a double omen and Zeus thundered from a clear sky (20.98-121); the present thunder answers that prayer at the critical moment, and the suitors 'change colour' (etrapeto, Monro: 'changed colour'). The epithet ankylomētēs, 'of crooked (devious) counsel', belongs to Cronos, who swallowed his children and castrated his father (Hesiod, Theogony 137-8, 168); Monro records Nauck's suggestion that the original reading was ankylomētis and that the manuscript G supports it. The epithet is pointed here: it is the son of the cunning god who sends the sign to the most cunning of mortals, polymētis Odysseus.

title: The shot through the axes
greek: πελέκεων δ' οὐκ ἤμβροτε πάντων πρώτης στειλειῆς (pelekeōn d' ouk ēmbrote pantōn prōtēs steileiēs)
short: Without rising from his stool Odysseus shoots, missing 'none of the axes at the tip of the handle', and the bronze-weighted arrow passes clean through and out.
body: The steileiē is the handle or haft of an axe. Monro takes prōtē steileiē as 'the top of the handle', construed with ēmbrote, 'did not miss the haft-end of any of the axes', and he insists that thuraze here means simply 'out, forth' from the axe-heads, with no reference to a door. Placing the arrow 'on the elbow' (epi pēchei) means resting it on the middle of the bow where the two horns join. The fact that he shoots seated, 'from the very chair' (autothen ek diphroio), stresses the ease of the feat after the suitors' laborious failures. Odysseus' words to Telemachus that 'the stranger brings no shame on you' (21.424-5) use elenchein, 'disgrace', the verb Eurymachus feared (21.329).

title: 'Song and lyre, the accompaniments of a feast'
greek: μολπῇ καὶ φόρμιγγι· τὰ γάρ τ' ἀναθήματα δαιτός (molpēi kai phorminggi: ta gar t' anathēmata daitos)
short: Odysseus grimly announces that it is time for 'supper' and then for other sport with music; the line quotes the poem's first description of the suitors' feasting.
body: Anathēmata, literally 'things set up', means 'delights' or 'ornaments' of the feast; the same line describes the suitors' pleasures in Book I (1.152), where Phemius sings for them. Monro calls 'supper in daylight' an oxymoron, a supper while it is still light being a contradiction in terms: the 'supper' really meant is the slaughter. The 'song and lyre' that follow the killing will also be literal, for Odysseus orders a sham wedding dance to hide the deed from the town (23.130-52). The scene closes with the silent signal of Odysseus' brows, and Telemachus arming at his father's side, the first time the two stand together in the hall as fighters.
